item.title: Jaiswal: India examining Hasina extradition request under established procedure
item.description:
India’s Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal has said that the extradition request for former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who was sentenced to death for crimes against humanity and is currently in India, is being examined according to established procedures.
He made the statement during the Indian Ministry of External Affairs’ weekly briefing on Wednesday.
Asked about Sheikh Hasina’s possible return to Bangladesh on December 16, Randhir Jaiswal said: “This is a matter between the former prime minister and the Bangladesh government. We have nothing more to say about it.”
Regarding the extradition request for Sheikh Hasina, he said: “The extradition request is being examined according to our established procedure (prevailing rules). However, the matter of any citizen who wishes to return to their country voluntarily, including with travel documents, is separate from the extradition request.”
Regarding the deterioration of the law and order situation in Bangladesh and allegations of attacks on Hindus, he said: “We are concerned about incidents of violence against minorities in Bangladesh. We urge the Bangladesh government to conduct thorough investigations into these incidents and bring the perpetrators to justice.”
Meanwhile, citing a person named Syed Mozammel Ali, who identifies himself as Sheikh Hasina’s spokesperson, a Reuters report published on Tuesday (November 24) said that ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina wants to return to Bangladesh on December 16, Victory Day.
After spending more than 2 years in exile in India, she has urged the government to arrange an aircraft of the state-flag carrier Biman Bangladesh Airlines for her return to the country.

item.title: Digital Duty of Care Act passes in Australia. Opposition say the law is ‘authoritarian’
item.description:
Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.

The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

Australian online law falls in line with EU and British legislation

The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”

Opposition leader vows to repeal ‘authoritarian’ law

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.”

“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy.”

The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

“Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23.

“My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added.

The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

—Rod Mcguirk, Associated Press

item.title: Settlers smash foundations of Palestinian family's homes in West Bank
item.description:
By Pesha Magid

JALOUD, West Bank, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Militant Israeli settlers smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the West Bank on Thursday, after settler attacks prevented the family from returning to them in defiance of an Israeli court order.

Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the hilltop two-storey houses on either side of a road in the village of Jaloud at around 1 a.m. and spending about an hour damaging the houses. The family said it had been forced out months ago.

item.description:

CAIRO, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Hamas chief Khalil Al-Hayya said on Thursday the group was not prepared to withstand continued Israeli attacks, after local medics said Israeli strikes killed at least 10 people in Gaza, including the Hamas-appointed deputy minister of education.

item.title: Pakistan Shaheens cruise into Asia Cup Rising Stars final with five-wicket win over Bangladesh ‘A’
item.description:
Pakistan Shaheens produced a composed five-wicket victory over Bangladesh ‘A’ in the second semi-final of the Asia Cup Rising Stars on Friday, chasing down a target of 233 with 28 balls to spare to book their place in Sunday’s final against Sri Lanka ‘A’.

The defending champions reached 233-5 in 45.2 overs after Bangladesh ‘A’ had posted 232-8 in their 50 overs. Hasan Nawaz, who made 62 and claimed two wickets, was named player of the match.

The chase was shaped by a measured third-wicket partnership between Hasan and Shahzaib Khan, who steadied the innings after Pakistan had lost both openers inside the first five overs. Shahzaib made 50 from 85 deliveries, while Hasan’s 91-ball 62 included three fours and three sixes.

Pakistan’s start had been unsettled by Bangladesh seamer Ripon Mondol, who removed the openers early and left the Shaheens needing to rebuild.

Hasan countered with calculated aggression, including a six off Iqbal Hossain Emon that eased the early pressure, while Shahzaib concentrated on occupying the crease and rotating the strike.

The pair took the total to 128 before Hasan was trapped leg-before by Md Rubel in the 31st over. Shahzaib continued to anchor the innings, bringing up his half-century before falling in the 35th over to an excellent diving catch by substitute fielder Rizwan at midwicket off Rakibul Hasan.

With the innings requiring fresh impetus, captain Abdul Samad and Farhan Yousaf took charge. Samad struck 44 from 33 balls, adding momentum with forceful strokes through the leg side, while Farhan remained unbeaten on 46 from 39 deliveries.

Their partnership carried Pakistan through a testing middle phase, with the required rate kept within reach despite a couple of quiet overs and a near run-out involving Farhan.

Samad’s dismissal, with the target in sight, did little to derail the chase. Farhan kept his composure, declining unnecessary risks and ensuring the innings moved forward. Pakistan crossed the line in 45.2 overs, with Rohail Nazir alongside Farhan when the winning run was completed.

Earlier, Bangladesh ‘A’ had been lifted by a superb unbeaten 103 from Shahadat Hossain, whose innings rescued a side that had struggled for momentum in the opening half.

He faced 118 balls, hitting seven fours and three sixes, and shared a 95-run third-wicket partnership with Mahidul Islam Ankon to give Bangladesh a platform.

Pakistan’s new-ball bowlers made early inroads, with Ali Raza dismissing both openers inside the first five overs.

Bangladesh made a cautious start and reached 41-2 after 13 overs, before Shahadat and Ankon rebuilt through patience and selective attacking shots. Ankon contributed 30, helping Shahadat settle before the partnership was broken.

Shahadat then found another useful ally in SM Meherob, with the pair adding a half-century for the sixth wicket. Meherob made 28 from 36 balls, but Pakistan struck twice in the 41st over when Hasan dismissed Meherob and Rubel in quick succession.

Sufyan Moqim was central to Pakistan’s recovery, finishing with 3-29 from his 10 overs and preventing Bangladesh from accelerating during the middle overs. Hasan took 2-30, while Raza also claimed two wickets.

Shahadat’s late surge, including a six to bring up his hundred in the final over, pushed Bangladesh beyond 230, but the total proved insufficient against Pakistan’s steady response.

The Shaheens’ disciplined chase ensured that Shahadat’s determined century went in vain and kept their title defence on course.

WASHINGTON: The United Nations on Wednesday launched its annual 16 Days of Activism campaign against gender-based violence, urging governments and societies to speak out against abuse, believe survivors and demand justice.

“Speak Out. Believe Survivors. De­­m­­and Justice,” read the message iss­ued by the UN to mark the first day of the global campaign, which runs until Dec 10, Human Rights Day. The campaign warned that too many survivors of violence and online harassment still face silence, disbelief and victim-blaming, allowing perpetrators to escape accountability.

“Every unanswered call for help, every dismissed report, and every unpunished act of violence” strengthens the web of impunity, the UN message said. It urged people to challenge attitudes that excuse violence, listen to survivors without judgment and respect their choices. Governments were asked to strengthen and enforce laws, fund support services and hold perpetrators and institutions accountable.

The campaign comes amid mounting concerns over violence against women in the digital and physical worlds, particularly in countries where social restrictions and inadequate protection systems discourage victims from seeking help.

A UN report on Pakistan, released on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on Nov 25, warned that online harassment was increasingly spilling into the physical world, contributing to femicide, suicide, physical violence and loss of employment.

The findings also showed how deeply entrenched social attitudes discourage women from challenging harassment. A survey in Pakistan found that 54pc of women believed women should leave their jobs if they faced harassment, while 83pc acknowledged that men often got away with harassing women.

The report said online abuse was not merely driving women and girls away from digital spaces but was also affecting their participation in professional and public life. It raised concerns about the response of companies, noting that most lacked clear policies to prevent and address online gender-based violence, while existing policies were often poorly implemented.

UN findings on attitudes in South Asia, including India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, pointed to a wider climate in which victims of harassment could face pressure to withdraw from public and professional life rather than expect perpetrators to be held accountable. The report also highlighted the global scale of violence. In the Arab states, 60pc of women internet users reported experiencing online violence.

Worldwide, an estimated 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2024 — an average of 137 every day, or one every 10 minutes — according to figures released by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime and UN Women.

The UN has urged women facing on­­­­line abuse to cut off contact with pe­­­r­­­p­­etrators and report online harassment, while calling on governments and technology companies to strengthen protections and accountability. The campaign’s launch also coincided with a renewed warning from UN Women about the deteriorating situation of women and girls in Afghanistan, where the risks of violence are increasing even as essential support services are disappearing because of funding cuts. In a statement marking the start of the campaign, UN Women Afghanistan urged governments and donors to increase support for Afghan women’s organisations, describing them as an essential lifeline for women and girls facing mounting social, economic and humanitarian pressures.

“Just as the risks of violence agai­nst women and girls are growing, the services they depend on are disappearing because of aid cuts,” said Su­­s­­an Ferguson, UN Women’s Special Representative in Afghanistan.

The UN said women’s organisations were particularly important in reaching survivors and providing services in circumstances where restrictions and economic hardship had sharply reduced their options.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

item.title: Dhaka Elevated Expressway: 81pc completed, Panthakunja ramp likely to open soon, Kamalapur section by June
item.description:
Eighty-one per cent of the construction work on the Dhaka Elevated Expressway has been completed, with the partially operational expressway already easing travel across the capital.

The Bangladesh Bridge Authority (BBA) says that once the entire expressway becomes operational, vehicles will be able to travel directly from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka to various areas, including Kutubkhali in Jatrabari, Kamalapur and Moghbazar.

The expressway is being constructed from Kawla, south of the airport, to Kutubkhali on the Dhaka-Chattogram Highway, with the aim of reducing traffic congestion in the capital.

The section from Kawla to Farmgate was opened to traffic on 3 September 2023, while the down ramp adjacent to the FDC rail gate was opened on 20 March 2024.

Dhaka–Chattogram in 3 hours: Tk 1.25 trillion expressway planned

A visit to the construction site near Sonargaon Link Road on 25 November found work underway. Workers said they worked from 7:00 am to evening. In addition to their basic wages, they received extra payment for overtime work.

However, conversations with several workers revealed that their numbers had declined somewhat compared with the previous month. Previously, 100 workers were employed under one engineer and 70 under another. For about a month, the number of workers has remained between 40 and 50.

Sources at the Bridge Authority said efforts were underway to open the Panthakunja ramp in Dhaka next January. Vehicles will be able to enter the expressway through this ramp, but will not be able to exit through it.

On 10 November, Bridge Division Secretary Mohammad Abdur Rouf told Prothom Alo that the contractor had been instructed to complete construction up to Kamalapur by June next year. He said the section was expected to become operational by June.

The government aims to open the entire expressway by December 2028 after completing all construction work.

Dhaka Elevated Expressway work stalled, no idea when it will resume

A PPP project

The Dhaka Elevated Expressway is a major project undertaken under a public-private partnership (PPP). It is the country's first elevated expressway project. The project is being implemented by the Bangladesh Bridge Authority. The First Dhaka Elevated Expressway (FDEE) Company Limited was formed to construct and operate it.

The project cost is Tk 89.4 billion. Under the agreement, the government will provide the investor with Tk 24.13 billion as viability gap funding (VGF), equivalent to 27 per cent of the estimated project cost. The construction company will invest the remaining amount. It will collect tolls for 25 years. The government will receive a share of the toll revenue based on the number of vehicles using the expressway.

The government will pay its share in three instalments during the construction period and another three instalments during the operational period. So far, the government has paid over Tk 10.68 billion to the investor in the first and second instalments.

Including the ramps, the expressway is approximately 47 kilometres long. Of this, around 20 kilometres comprise the main elevated road, while the remaining 27 kilometres consist of ramps. There are 31 ramps in total.

Metro rail extension to Kamalapur 85pc complete, service set to begin in July

Two Chinese companies are investors in the Dhaka Elevated Expressway. China Shandong International Economic and Technical Cooperation Group (CSI) holds an 80 per cent stake, while Sinohydro Corporation holds the remaining 20 per cent.

Initially, more than half of the project's shares were held by Thailand-based Italian-Thai Development Public Company Limited. However, following financial difficulties and disputes among the partners over shareholding that eventually reached the court, the Thai company lost its stake in the project.

According to the Bridge Authority, the project agreement was signed on 19 January 2011, while a revised agreement was signed on 15 December 2013. Construction began in January 2020. The expressway was supposed to become operational within three and a half years of the start of construction. However, financial difficulties and disputes over shareholding repeatedly disrupted the work on the Dhaka Elevated Expressway.

The project was subsequently scheduled for completion by June 2024, but that deadline was not met. In total, 15 years have passed since the project agreement was signed, while six years have elapsed since construction began. The new completion deadline has been set for 31 December 2028.

The expressway is being constructed in three phases. The first phase, stretching 7.45 kilometres, runs from Kawla, south of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, to Banani Railway Station. The second phase, covering 5.85 kilometres, extends from Banani Railway Station to Moghbazar Railway Crossing. The third phase, spanning 6.43 kilometres, runs from Moghbazar Railway Crossing to the Dhaka-Chattogram Highway at Kutubkhali.

As of September 2026, 100 per cent of the first phase, 87 per cent of the second phase and more than 22 per cent of the third phase had been completed.

Padma Bridge link: Eight-lane road planned via Postogola to Gabtoli to avoid Dhaka traffic

Project official Mohammad Golam Mortuza said the project cost remained unchanged at Tk 89.4 billion despite the extension of the deadline. "The amount has not increased. The calculation of the 25-year toll collection period began in 2020," he said.

Jahangir Alam regularly travels along the expressway from the airport towards Tejgaon. He said it takes him around 15 minutes to reach Farmgate by bus from the airport.

Like Jahangir Alam, many people use the expressway. However, allegations that FDEE has underreported the number of vehicles using it, are currently under investigation.

Residents of the capital are now waiting to see when the project will be completed.

Bridge Division Secretary Abdur Rouf said, "The project is facing various challenges. Construction is taking longer than expected. There were problems on our side as well. Land acquisition in some areas took time. Work at Panthakunja remained suspended for a year."

He said vehicle movement would increase once the section up to Kamalapur became operational. This would also generate revenue for the government.

item.title: Deputy Speaker calls for amending Article 70, independent Parliament Secretariat
item.description:
Deputy Speaker of Parliament Kayesar Kamal has called for amending Article 70 of the Constitution to give lawmakers greater freedom to vote independently and establishing an independent parliamentary secretariat to strengthen the Jatiya Sangsad’s ability to hold the government accountable.

Speaking at a seminar in Dhaka on Thursday, he said Bangladesh’s parliamentary history had seen both democratic progress and serious setbacks, with some parliaments strengthening democratic institutions while others had weakened them and become rubber stamps for the executive.

The current parliament has an opportunity to correct those mistakes and make the institution more effective, he said.

Kamal identified Articles 70, 76, 77 and 79 of the Constitution as requiring attention. He called for revising Article 70 to ensure that MPs can exercise greater independence while retaining safeguards on matters of national interest.

He also stressed the need to enact a law under Article 76(3) to make parliamentary standing committees more independent and effective in scrutinising the executive.

“Unless that law is passed, we cannot oversee or scrutinise executive functions effectively,” he said.

On Article 79, the Deputy Speaker called for an independent parliamentary secretariat staffed by its own officials, rather than relying on civil servants deputed from other government offices.

He also urged competent professionals, particularly young people, to enter politics and contribute to strengthening Parliament.

Kamal was speaking at a seminar titled ‘How Can the Jatiya Sangsad Be Made More Efficient and Effective,’ organised by Dhaka Tribune with the support of the Royal Norwegian Embassy in Dhaka. The event brought together policymakers, political representatives, academics and experts to discuss parliamentary institutions, democratic governance and accountability.

Political scientist Professor Rounaq Jahan said many of the reforms being discussed had already been recommended in a 2012 study on Parliament, but few had been implemented.

She said MPs should prioritise national legislation and oversight instead of focusing mainly on development projects in their constituencies. However, this would require political parties and their leaders to clarify the division of responsibilities between MPs and local government representatives.

“Unless it is the party decision, unless it is a decision by the political leadership, you cannot expect individual MPs to suddenly change their priorities,” she said.

Jahan also called for a parliamentary code of conduct, annual disclosure of MPs’ financial assets and declarations of conflicts of interest.

Saiful Alam Milan, a member central executive committee of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami and a lawmaker from Dhaka-12, said the July uprising had created an opportunity to rebuild Parliament after 15 years of authoritarian rule, during which elections lost credibility and the legislature largely became a rubber stamp for government decisions.

He criticised parliamentary procedures that allow the Speaker to waive requirements for advance notice and circulation of bills. Citing the passage of 94 bills in 25 working days during the first session, he said two civil service bills had been passed in just eight minutes without discussion.

He also questioned the passage of the Invest Bangladesh Bill on the same day it was approved by the Cabinet, without scrutiny by a parliamentary committee.

“Parliamentary safeguards must be protected as an institution, regardless of who holds power,” he said.

Milan called for opposition representation in the chairmanship of standing committees, at least two Opposition Days in every parliamentary session, a citizen petition system and public hearings by parliamentary committees. He also urged Parliament to limit the use of presidential ordinances and implement the July Charter.

“A strong opposition is not a threat to a strong government. It is a safeguard against a weak democracy,” he said.↳

Dr Badiul Alam Majumder, founder-secretary of Citizens for Good Governance (Sujan), said Parliament’s responsibilities included lawmaking, oversight of the executive, financial scrutiny and public deliberation. He stressed that the people, not Parliament, were sovereign under the Constitution.

He called for stricter eligibility requirements for MPs, proper scrutiny of candidates’ declarations of assets and liabilities, and greater representation of women and different sections of society in Parliament. He also proposed laws on parliamentary privileges and MPs’ codes of conduct, including mandatory declarations of conflicts of interest and annual financial disclosures.

“These are people's representatives. They belong to political parties, but they must work in the interests of the people rather than the party,” he said.

Badiul Alam Majumder said the July Charter, signed by all parties with a written commitment to its full implementation, had clearly stipulated that four important parliamentary committee chairmanships should go to the opposition. However, although the 13th Parliament had formed 50 standing committees, only one chairmanship—the Public Accounts Committee—had been given to the opposition. He said the commitment had not been reflected in practice and stressed that the agreed provisions should be implemented.

Dr Debapriya Bhattacharya, a distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said the country's parliamentary history showed how two-thirds majorities had sometimes been used to undermine democracy. The current parliament, which also enjoys such a majority, should learn from that experience.

“The first lesson to making an effective parliament is possibly how to harness the two-thirds majority,” he said.

He called for making better use of existing parliamentary mechanisms, including standing committees, and increasing opposition participation in their work. He also proposed reforming Article 70 to allow MPs to vote independently, except on confidence motions, budgetary matters and international treaties.

Bhattacharya further said public hearings outside Parliament could also help make lawmakers more accountable to citizens, he said.

Norwegian Ambassador to Bangladesh Håkon Arald Gulbrandsen distinguished between parliamentary efficiency and effectiveness. Efficiency, he said, meant using parliamentary time and resources properly, while effectiveness meant fulfilling constitutional and democratic responsibilities.

He identified institutional independence, strong parliamentary committees, meaningful opposition participation and quality debates as important conditions for an effective legislature. MPs must also have adequate support, time and access to information to scrutinise government policies and hold ministers accountable.

The ambassador said a balance was needed between preventing disruptions that waste parliamentary time and allowing protests and heated debates as legitimate forms of democratic representation.

NCP Joint Convener and lawmaker Nusrat Tabassum Joty, constitutional expert Rashna Imam, and independent politician Tasnim Jara, among others, spoke at the seminar.

Zafar Sobhan, editor of Counterpoint, moderated the seminar.

Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,371 as 8 die in 24 hours
item.description:
The measles outbreak has claimed 8 more lives in Bangladesh in the 24 hours up to 8am on Thursday, taking the total death toll from confirmed cases and suspected measles to 1,371 since March 15, 2026.
Of the latest fatalities, 7 were reported among children with measles-like symptoms, while 1 was from a confirmed measles case, according to a press release issued by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) on Thursday.
The DGHS recorded 1,109 suspected and confirmed measles cases during the same period.
With the latest fatalities, the death toll from suspected measles reached 1,265 since March 15. Meanwhile, deaths from confirmed measles cases stood at 106, including 1 reported in the 24 hours up to 8am on Thursday.
According to the release, 1,007 suspected measles cases were reported during the latest 24-hour period, taking the total to 261,535 since March 15.
Another 102 confirmed cases were reported during the same period, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to 26,476.
Between March 15 and November 26, a total of 234,280 patients with suspected measles were admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 225,568 were discharged, the release added.

item.title: Hasina’s ex-deputy press secretary Sakhawat Moon, two others sent to jail
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Thursday sent KM Sakhawat Moon, former deputy press secretary ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina, and two others to jail in a case filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act with Mohammadpur Police Station.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Kamal Uddin passed the order following a police petition, said state prosecutor Shamsuddoha Sumon.
The other accused are former Madaripur deputy commissioner Md Ilias Hossain, 50, and tax lawyer Sufi Md Al Mamun, 50.
Earlier, Mohammadpur Police Station Sub-Inspector Md Masudur Rahman and also the investigation officer in the case produced the three accused before the court and sought an order to keep them in jail.
In his petition, the investigation officer said preliminary findings had revealed evidence of the accused's involvement in the incident. As the investigation was ongoing, he argued that they needed to remain in custody until its completion. Police also said a remand petition against the accused was being submitted.
According to the case statement, several male and female members of the activities-banned Awami League, Jubo League and Chhatra League brought out an unauthorised procession in front of Lalmatia Women's College at around 12:50am on November 26.
Local residents detained the accused, and police later arrived at the scene and took them into custody.
Citing information obtained during interrogation, police said the accused were detained while displaying banners of the activities-banned Awami League, Jubo League and Chhatra League and chanting provocative slogans against the government.
During the incident, 20 to 25 unidentified people fled the scene.
Police filed the case with Mohammadpur Police Station over the incident.

item.title: Myanmar won’t comply with ‘inappropriate’ parts of genocide ruling
item.description:
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing said his government would not comply with “inappropriate” aspects of a UN court ruling that the state committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, state media said Thursday.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) last week delivered a searing guilty verdict, finding Myanmar forces systematically killed, raped and destroyed property of civilians from the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in western Rakhine state.
It ordered Myanmar authorities to prosecute and punish anyone suspected of perpetrating genocide, compensate survivors and facilitate safe passage home for refugees -- more than 700,000 of whom fled to Bangladesh.
Speaking during a meeting Wednesday, coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing said “Myanmar would take the actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate,” state media said.
The ex-general commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering an ongoing civil war.
Min Aung Hlaing was installed this year as civilian president following deeply restricted elections.
In his first publicized comments on the ICJ ruling, which determined state rather than individual responsibility, he called the case a “one-sided accusation” against Myanmar.
He also said the “term ‘genocide’ had seriously affected the country’s reputation,” according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar.
“As the country’s leader, he considered himself primarily responsible for all matters occurring in the country and would not accept any actions that undermined the nation,” it added.
While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts.
The ruling was the first in the ICJ’s 80-year history in which its judges determined that a state committed genocide.
Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, the court found.
Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, it said, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population -- a key test for genocide.
The court ordered several remedies, including that Myanmar authorities must “facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within the country or abroad.
Most of Rakhine state, from where the Rohingya fled, is now controlled by the Arakan Army, an ethnic minority rebel group fighting the military.
More than one million Rohingya currently live in Cox’s Bazar, across the border in neighbouring Bangladesh, now the world’s biggest refugee camp.
The court said the Rohingya are entitled to “adequate compensation” for the harms caused by the genocide.
It gave Myanmar two years to set the amount and method of compensation, and will then determine whether the proposal is sufficient.
Authorities must also “return or replace in kind all individual and collective property” that was lost in the crackdown, and offer “physical and psychological rehabilitation,” the ICJ ruled.
Judges told Myanmar it must promptly investigate anyone suspected of committing genocide, noting previous probes into atrocities by state actors were insufficient.
Myanmar has always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted an armed insurgency after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.
But the ICJ ruling dismissed Myanmar’s argument that it was carrying out counter-insurgency operations.
On Friday, the Myanmar government described the ICJ decision as unfair and “a great disappointment.”
The ICJ case was brought by The Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to file suit against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthi-held capital hit after group targets Riyadh
item.description:
Houthi media reported a series of Saudi airstrikes against territories held by the Iran-backed group, including the capital Sanaa, on Thursday, hours after it struck Riyadh.
The exchanges between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen have become near-daily in the country’s revived civil war, which first began more than a decade ago.
The coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said during the night that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital of Riyadh, where residents and an AFP journalist heard an explosion.
It also said it had destroyed a cruise missile launched towards the west of the country and a drone in the Jeddah region, on the Red Sea.
“The air force of the Saudi enemy today launched a series of strikes at the capital Sanaa,” the Houthis’ press agency reported on Thursday morning.
An AFP journalist in Sanaa reported seeing smoke in the area of the airport. The Houthi news outlet Almasirah reported that the strikes targeted a factory and warehouses in Bani al-Harith.
Later on Thursday, residents of the key Houthi-controlled port of Hodeida told AFP they had heard jets overflying the city and loud explosions.
The Houthis said the day before they had struck two Saudi ports on the Red Sea, after Saudi strikes on Hodeida.
The coalition, meanwhile, said it had brought down a Houthi projectile targeting Jazan that had caused light damage and no civilian casualties.
Yemen’s civil war burst back into life in July, bringing to an end a years-long truce that began in 2022.
The fighting has intensified since September, with the Houthis making significant territorial gains and bearing down on the temporary seat of the government in Aden.
Since then, the group has frequently struck Saudi oil facilities and other infrastructure, including airports and Riyadh’s financial district. Those attacks have killed 26 people, according to Saudi authorities.
The Houthis have reported hundreds killed by Saudi strikes “since the beginning of the Saudi escalation.”

item.title: Kim Jong Un inspects nuclear sites, vows to build more nukes
item.description:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured factories that make nuclear material, along with a research institute, and pressed for the wider use of tactical nuclear weapons, state media reported on Thursday.
The visit took place on Wednesday, but the state news agency KCNA did not provide the location of the sites. Photos showed Kim walking between rows of what appeared to be centrifuges for enriching uranium. Analysts also spotted small, standardized tactical warheads such as the Hwasan-31.
Kim said North Korea’s production capacity for nuclear material is being steadily expanded. He said tactical weapons should be used in different areas and for different missions, citing the danger from a hostile state on his border, referring to neighbor South Korea.
He also accused the United States of encouraging its allies to seek nuclear-powered submarines and to share nuclear weapons.
“Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony,” Kim said, adding that he would treat any attempt to deny North Korea’s nuclear status, which was written into its constitution in 2023, as a declaration of war.
Kim said Pyongyang would not seek approval from other countries.
Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University, said the visit signals Kim’s desire to change the circumstances of any future talks on North Korea’s weapons programs.
“This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: ‘denuclearization talks’ are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a ‘nuclear state versus nuclear state’ basis,” he told Reuters news agency.
South Korean news agency Yonhap said this was Kim’s fourth visit to a nuclear facility since September 2024. It came about a week after US President Donald Trump visited China for the Apec summit, where Kim did not publicly respond to an offer to meet.
Trump told the New York Post that Kim had not ignored it and that the timing was wrong.
Meanwhile, the South Korean Defense Ministry said Pyongyang must stop justifying nuclear development and implement UN Security Council resolutions prohibiting its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.

item.title: Indonesia mine flood death toll rises to 13, with over a dozen missing
item.description:
The death toll from flooding in an illegal gold mine on Indonesia’s Java island, following heavy rain, rose to 13, a rescue official said Thursday, with more than a dozen others still missing.
Mining accidents are common across the mineral-rich Southeast Asian archipelago, especially on unlicensed sites where safety protocols are lax and often ignored.
The mine was flooded when a nearby river overflowed after a torrential downpour on Monday, trapping the miners inside.
Thirteen workers were found dead, while 13 others are still missing as of Thursday morning, local search and rescue chief Desiana Kartika Bahari said in a statement.
Photos and video footage shared by the agency on Thursday showed rescuers working well into the night with headlamps and ropes to evacuate victim remains in the dark.
The workers were trapped in two pits which are still flooded three days following the incident, Desiana told local broadcaster Kompas TV Thursday.
Efforts to pump the water out of the pits were unsuccessful due in part to downpours that hit the area.
“The structure (of the pits) is like a narrow staircase leading down. This makes the evacuation difficult,” Desiana said, adding that rescuers were helped by some miners.
Poor lighting and slippery terrain also challenged rescuers, she said in a statement.
West Java police chief Hengki, who like many Indonesians has one name, pledged an investigation late Wednesday.
Eleven miners were able to leave safely before the shafts flooded, said West Java police spokesman Hendra Rochmawan.
Authorities were only alerted to the trapped miners on Tuesday, he added.
In 2023, rescuers were unable to retrieve eight miners who were trapped inside a flooded illegal gold mine in Central Java province.
They were officially declared missing and presumed dead.
Six people were killed on Sulawesi island in 2021 after an illegal gold mine collapsed.
At least 16 people were killed two years earlier when another illegal gold mine on the island collapsed and buried the workers.

item.title: Egypt: Over 30 dead after fuel truck overturns near Cairo
item.description:
A fuel truck overturned on a packed highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, killing 31 people and injuring 21 more, according to Egyptian authorities.
The fuel tanker crash ignited a massive blaze on Ring Road in Giza’s Waraq district. The Ring Road encircles the greater Cairo metropolitan area.
Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were transported to nearby hospitals and added that the death toll could rise further. He said 39 ambulances are responding to the accident.
A massive fire broke out after the accident, with rescue workers pulling people from their vehicles. A large crowd gathered in the densely populated Waraq neighborhood amid the rescue efforts.
The blaze left at least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, charred.
An investigation has been launched into the crash, according to Egypt’s public prosecutor. DNA tests are being carried out to identify badly burned victims of the blaze.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his deepest condolences and sympathy to the victims and directed relevant authorities to provide necessary support to the families of the victims and the injured.
Other countries also reacted to the crash in Giza.
Italian Foreign Affairs Minister Antonio Tajani said he extended his “deepest solidarity to the victims’ families,” Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty “and to the Egyptian people, whom I count as friends, at this tragic time.”
Algerian Ambassador to Egypt Mohamed Sofiane Berrah also said the Embassy of Algeria in Cairo extended “its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathy to the sisterly Arab Republic of Egypt.”
Car accidents are frequent in Egypt due to poor road conditions, reckless driving and lax enforcement of safety rules.

item.title: India urges US to resolve tariff dispute in trade talks
item.description:
India’s commerce ministry said trade concerns should be addressed through ongoing talks with Washington, after the United States proposed raising tariffs on Indian goods to 17%.
“India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement,” the commerce ministry said late Wednesday, adding it was working towards an “early conclusion” of a deal.
“It has been India’s position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations,” the statement said.
The United States is India’s largest trade partner and the two countries reached an interim agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
But the US Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs days later, fueling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.
The two sides have been negotiating ever since.
On Wednesday, however, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production, Washington proposed a 17 percent rate on India.
“India engaged constructively throughout this investigation,” New Delhi added.
“In response... the Department of Commerce stated that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.”
The new tariffs face a period of public comment before taking effect.
The New Delhi-based Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) said offering lower tariffs under the trade pact was “deliberate bait” to pressure India.
“New Delhi must reject a one-sided trade deal and defend its industrial expansion sector-by-sector,” GTRI head Ajay Srivastava said in a report.
Neighboring Bangladesh meanwhile faces a proposed US tariff increase to 18%, which could affect its garment exports, a key source of revenue for the country.
“We hope that the US would not do anything that risks affecting our bilateral trade,” Dhaka’s Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir told The Daily Star newspaper on Thursday.
Dhaka-based economist Mohammad Abdur Razzaque, head of the Research and Policy Integration for Development thinktank, said that “higher tariffs would result in lower apparel demand in the US, reducing Bangladesh’s export earnings.”
“Bangladesh is already facing significant economic challenges including weakened economic growth and export prospects,” he added.

item.title: Home minister: Tough action if necessary to protect lives, property
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Thursday warned that law enforcement agencies would take tough measures if necessary to protect people's lives and property.
“No conspiracy by the party will be allowed to succeed. However, if necessary, law enforcement agencies will take the toughest measures in accordance with the law to protect the lives and property of people,” he said.
The minister made the remarks at a press briefing after a joint meeting of the BNP and its affiliated and associate organisations at the party's central office in Nayapaltan. BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi presided over the meeting.
Salahuddin Ahmed, a BNP Standing Committee member, said although many people are talking about political instability in the current context, he did not see any such situation in the country.
He said the politically irrelevant “fallen fascist force” had fled the country in the face of the mass uprising in July, which, he said, was stained with the blood of hundreds and thousands of martyrs.
The minister said the party might now identify itself as a “fugitive party”, adding that some of its recent activities had put its remaining underground networks in the country in trouble, while some people had been misled and fallen into its trap.
Salahuddin said the government had taken a principled decision to run the state democratically and had therefore instructed law enforcement agencies to exercise utmost patience.
“We did not want any bloodshed. Rather, people at home and abroad have appreciated the behaviour, sacrifices and patience of BNP as the ruling party,” he said.
He said the BNP was committed to democratic practices and had signed the July National Charter with the aim of building democratic institutions and ensuring that all political activities were conducted through democratic means.
Salahuddin said the trials of those accused of crimes against humanity were underway at the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT).
Those responsible for crimes against humanity would face trial individually and as an organisation under Article 47 of the Constitution and the amendments to the Anti-Terrorism Act, he said.
The minister said an investigation into the Awami League as an organisation over crimes against humanity is underway.
Once the investigation is completed, charges would be framed and a charge sheet submitted through the proper legal process, after which the tribunal would proceed in accordance with the law.
The fate of the former ruling force would then be determined in accordance with the tribunal's directives and the relevant legal provisions, he added.

item.title: Europe’s ‘double standards’ on Russia and Gaza an obstacle to partnerships, says Borrell at Chatham House’s Berlin conference
item.description:
Europe’s ‘double standards’ on Russia and Gaza an obstacle to partnerships, says Borrell at Chatham House’s Berlin conference News release thilton.drupal 27 November 2026

During a panel discussion at our 2026 conference, experts discussed Europe’s need to offer credibility in the face of attacks on multilateral institutions.

Europe must be credible and avoid ‘double standards’ as it seeks to build relations with Global South countries and other partners, said Josep Borrell, the former High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy of the European Commission, speaking on a panel at Chatham House’s Berlin Conference 2026. 

He said the recent meeting of presidents Xi, Trump and Putin in Shenzhen was ‘much worse’ than ‘a new Yalta’, in reference to the 1945 summit where Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill set out the post-war order. 

‘In Yalta, they built institutions, and here, the three of them attack institutions,’ he said.

Borrell argued that in this context, while Europe had a lot to offer the rest of the world, including on trade, it needed to maintain its credibility if it wanted to serve as an anchor of a ‘network that makes spheres of influence impossible.’  

He said:

‘We have to offer credibility, and there is an important thing for us: it’s not to show different standards. Not to show that in some cases we are in favour and others against. I’m talking about Gaza and the fact that many people around the world claim that we have been using double standards on that.’

‘We proclaim that we have values and we are acting according with our values, but these values have a variable geometry … We condemn strongly Russia aggression against Ukraine, but we say nothing about what’s going on on the Middle East. 

‘This is the proof that many countries around the world consider that our values are relative. And this is certainly a political obstacle.’

Shada Islam, a journalist and author speaking on the panel, added that the perception of inconsistency also applied to Venezuela and the US-Israeli war on Iran. 

She added that Europe’s ‘authoritarian impulse’ on migration policy and discussions about Islam also led to ‘disenchantment’ in the rest of the world.

‘The coarse and very damaging insults, innuendos etc. that are coming from many of our politicians … When the rest of the world hears that, there is also a certain degree of disenchantment, is the word I’d say, about Europe. People see those double standards more, I think, than they would if it was an external policy affair.’

Islam pointed out that some of the governments making the accusations of double standards were themselves ‘pretty authoritarian’ and ‘pretty much engaged in double standards too.’  She argued that Europe’s strategic assets were ‘people’ and ‘values.’

Outlining Europe’s partnership options, Borrell said: ‘I think partners should be chosen by shared interest in rules, not by geography or ideology.’ 

He pointed to three circles of partners: democracies with no current imperial ambitions such as Canada, Japan and the UK; ‘swing states’ such as India, Brazil, and the Gulf; and regional organizations such as ASEAN, the African Union and Mercosur. 

Z. Levent Gümrükçü, Türkiye’s Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, argued that Ankara was already a key part of Europe’s security infrastructure, as a member of NATO, the OECD and the Council of Europe. 

Gümrükçü said that the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act and ‘Made in Europe’ initiative seemed to suggest Europe was preparing to ‘build walls’ around its industry. 

He said: ‘From my point of view, this is wrong. I think the road ahead, the road forward should not be “made in EU”, but it should be “made with EU”.’

Borrell said that ‘Turkey has not received the attention that [it] deserves, and clearly [the] European Union has not been proactive in the relationship with Turkey.’

On this week’s episode of Independent Thinking, our experts discuss the outcome of the COP31 climate summit.

The conclusion of the COP31 talks in Antalya without a consensus agreement due to the absence of fossil fuels in the final document seemed to be a serious setback in the fight against climate change. But what is really happening in climate cooperation? Is reaching a consensus on a cover decision as important as concrete action? Developing nations’ efforts are under financial pressure, China has become both the biggest emitter and the leading power in renewables, and wars at energy choke points are clouding the picture. Can the consensus-based COP structure survive?
